title: Loss-Resilient Quantum Networking with Dicke Entanglement
authors: Bowen Wang, Hongyu Yang, Jiacheng Sun, Wanping Zhou, Jizhou Wu, Yunlong Xiao, Dian Wu, Jian Wu
abstract: Multipartite entanglement can endow a quantum network with capabilities unavailable classically, yet their evolution under progressively reduced physical and informational access remains largely unexplored. Here we realize the first eight-photon half-excitation Dicke state, with a fidelity of 0.922(11), and use it to implement two distinct network tasks: open-destination teleportation and quantum telecloning. An unknown state can be teleported from one agent to any of seven remote agents with fidelities of 0.926(7)-0.941(6), while seven approximate clones are distributed with a fidelity of 0.713(3), close to the optimal value of 5/7. The protocol remains above the classical limit under imperfect photon detection, transmission loss and missing information from participating agents, and outperforms the corresponding GHZ benchmarks. As fewer agents contribute, the teleportation fidelity falls through a stepwise hierarchy whose two extremes recover open-destination teleportation and optimal telecloning, connecting both tasks within a single operational framework. These results establish Dicke entanglement as a promising architecture for loss-resilient quantum networks, opening a route towards quantum technologies that retain useful functionality under realistic operating conditions.
summary: This paper experimentally realizes and tests the utility of eight-photon Dicke entanglement for quantum networking. It proves that this highly entangled state allows quantum tasks like teleportation and cloning to maintain functionality above classical bounds even when the network suffers from photon loss or missing agent data. The key finding is that the network performance degrades in a predictable, stepwise manner, confirming Dicke entanglement's promise for loss-resilient quantum technologies.
main_problem: The research addresses the challenge of maintaining quantum network functionality when subjected to physical imperfections such as photon loss, imperfect detection, or missing information from participating agents.
main_result: The study demonstrates that Dicke entanglement serves as a robust resource, enabling quantum tasks like open-destination teleportation and telecloning to remain above classical limits even under significant network impairments.
method: The authors experimentally generated and characterized an eight-photon Dicke state and implemented two network tasks, analyzing performance by systematically introducing controlled levels of channel loss and agent information loss.
model_or_system: The system utilizes an eight-photon half-excitation Dicke state, generated using spontaneous parametric down-conversion and distributed across eight spatial modes via a beam-splitter network.
key_observables: Fidelity of the generated state (0.922(11)), Open-Destination Teleportation (ODT) fidelity (0.926(7)-0.941(6)), and quantum telecloning fidelity (0.713(3)).
important_parameters: The analysis tracks performance relative to the classical limit (2/3) and the optimal telecloning fidelity (5/7), varying parameters include photon loss ($\gamma$) and the number of unavailable assisting agents.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to model channels with independent loss probability $\gamma$ and notes that equal fidelity does not guarantee operational equivalence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ODT protocol with unavailable agents, the experimental setup for state generation, and plots showing the fidelity hierarchy for both ODT and telecloning across varying loss/failure conditions.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical resource (Dicke state) and then systematically tests its utility by implementing and analyzing two key protocols (ODT and telecloning) under increasingly realistic and degraded operational conditions (loss, missing data).
why_interesting: The demonstration of a predictable, stepwise hierarchy in performance as resources fail provides a deep insight into the structural robustness of multipartite entanglement, which is highly relevant for designing fault-tolerant quantum communication protocols.
